title: No requests today
hookLine: on Shabbat the weekday requests are replaced by one blessing of the day's holiness
carry: already enough, just as it is

lines: ON SHABBAT, THE MIDDLE IS GONE.
cards: Help me understand this. Forgive me for that. Heal my friend.
Help with money. Fix this mess. A normal week can run on requests, and the weekday Amidah is built the same way.
This path walked through it earlier this year: a prayer of nineteen blessings, and the long middle is one request after another. Wisdom, forgiveness, healing, a good year's harvest, justice, peace.
Then Friday night comes, you open the prayer book to the same place, and the middle is gone.

teach.b: On Shabbat, the Amidah keeps its first three blessings, the praise, and its last three, the thanks and the peace. But the thirteen requests in the middle are taken out.
In their place goes a single blessing called kedushat hayom, the holiness of the day. So the Sabbath Amidah has seven blessings instead of nineteen. Why remove the requests?
The Talmud's answer is short: out of honor for Shabbat, the rabbis didn't want to weigh people down.
Later teachers add that asking for your needs means thinking about everything that's wrong, illness, debt, the harvest, and Shabbat isn't the day for that. The day isn't for fixing your life.
It's for living it as if it were already enough. There's a striking line in the Talmud about visiting the sick on Shabbat. You don't pray at length for their recovery.
Instead, the Talmud gives the words to say: it's Shabbat, we don't cry out; healing will come soon. The day itself is the comfort. That doesn't mean people stop caring on Shabbat, or stop hoping.
Hearts still carry their worries in, and some of the rabbis' sources struggle with how much request is allowed.

But the shape of the prayer makes a point. Six days a week you're a person with needs. One day a week, the prayer treats you as a person who has what they need: coming before God not to ask, but just to be there.
The middle blessing is the day itself.

how: The Shabbat Amidah has seven blessings: the first three and last three of the weekday Amidah, with the thirteen petitions replaced by one central blessing for the holiness of the day, worded differently at each Shabbat service.

o: the holiness of the day: Shabbat's one middle blessing
the closing prayer that ends the Sabbath at nightfall
the thirteen requests said on Shabbat mornings

s: the Shabbat Amidah adds extra requests
it removes the thirteen requests and adds one blessing of the day.
the first and last three blessings stay the same on Shabbat
the rabbis said Shabbat shouldn't be weighed down by needs
so the day itself becomes the middle blessing.

games.q: it's Shabbat. you visit a friend who is sick. what does the Talmud suggest you say?
o: it's Shabbat, we don't cry out; healing will come soon.
games.why: the Talmud's words:it's Shabbat, we don't cry out, and healing is near. the day itself is the comfort.

practice: For these two minutes, don't ask for a single thing, not from God, not from yourself: no fix, no plan, no wish.
When a request comes up, and it will, notice it, set it down beside you, and come back to the breath, just being in what is.

wordCard.voice: Kedushat hayom. The holiness of the day: the single blessing that replaces the weekday's thirteen requests on Shabbat.
